headline: Bayer will pay $7.25 billion. It still says Roundup is safe.
summary: A Missouri judge approved a $7.25 billion settlement Friday between Bayer and people who say its weed killer Roundup gave them lymphoma. Payments run up to 21 years and average $10,000 to $165,000 a person. Bayer denies Roundup causes cancer. In June the Supreme Court said Bayer can't be sued in state courts for failing to warn.

cover_question.q: If it causes cancer, why sell it?

cover_answer: Still in dispute. WHO says probably, the EPA not likely.
table_question: Is paying to end a fight the same as admitting you were wrong?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: A company that makes weed spray agreed to pay a lot of money to people who got very sick after using it for years, mostly on farms. The company says the spray didn't do it, but it is paying so the arguing stops. It's like chipping in for a broken window when nobody agrees who threw the ball. Spray is a grown-up job, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: They will hear ‘sick’ and check the garage. One line about the yard spray settles it.
5-7.why_long: At six the world is what is in reach, so 200,000 lawsuits become one question: the spray bottle in our garage. The script answers that first, then the broken window makes ‘paying without agreeing you did it’ a playground thing. Expect ‘did the spray make people die?’ Say some got very sick, and that spray is a grown-up job.

8-12.script: Roundup has killed weeds since 1974. Some 200,000 people say it gave them a cancer called lymphoma and sued Bayer, its maker. A Missouri judge approved a deal Friday: Bayer pays up to $7.25 billion and the suits end, like a referee stopping the match and setting the score. Bayer never admits a thing.
8-12.why: Someone pays, nobody is found guilty. The referee explains it.
8-12.why_long: A twelve-year-old is sorting rules from outcomes, and a settlement breaks the rule they expect: someone pays, nobody is found guilty. The referee who ends the match is the mechanism, and 1974 to Friday is the chain. Expect ‘so did they do it or not?’ A couple dozen juries split. This deal ends the rest without a verdict.

13-17.script: If Bayer says Roundup is safe, why pay $7.25 billion? In June the Supreme Court said Bayer can't be sued in state courts for failing to warn, since federal rules don't require a cancer label. That weakened the lawsuits. Second: WHO says probably, the EPA says not likely. Who should the label trust?
13-17.why: A denial next to a $7.25 billion payment. Ask what the money means.
13-17.why_long: A fourteen-year-old can hold two true things: Bayer denies the link, and Bayer pays $7.25 billion. The script adds the Supreme Court ruling that changed the odds, so the money reads as a bet, not a confession. Kuhn calls that argument practice. Expect ‘so the company bought its way out?’ The patients' lawyers split on that.

5-7.q: Is the weed spray at our house bad?
5-7.a: The kind sold for yards changed its recipe. Spray is a grown-up job anyway. You don't touch it.

8-12.q: If it causes cancer, why sell it?
8-12.a: Nobody has settled that. WHO says probably; the EPA says not likely.
People with lymphoma who used Roundup. $10,000 to $165,000 each.

13-17.q: If it's safe, why pay $7 billion?
13-17.a: Certainty. A fixed bill for 200,000 claims, and no admission.

13-17.q: Does this mean Roundup causes cancer?
13-17.a: Unsettled. WHO said probably in 2015. The EPA says not likely.
